cards.explanation: The answer is sleep. David swears, “I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids…” (Psalm 132:4). He names his eyes AND his eyelids, like he's covering every angle, friends. I would last about four minutes before my chef's hat slid down over my face.

The answer is a place for the LORD. David swears he won't rest “…until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob.” Look at what he's hunting for, friends: a dwelling for the LORD, and nothing about a nicer place for himself. That's an oath with the focus in the right spot.

The answer is worship. The group says, “Let us go to His dwelling place; let us worship at His footstool.” They're not just saying it to the air. They're inviting each other, which I love, because worship is better with company. Even a stamper who works alone like me ends up with a crowd around the cookie box eventually.

The answer is to His resting place. The song says, “Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your strength.” Strength and rest in the same sentence, friends. I like a sentence that can hold both.

The answer is False. The verse says, “May Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and Your saints shout for joy.” The song asks for joy, not tears, friends. The only thing getting shouted in this verse is happiness, and I'd be shouting too.

The answer is reject him. The song says, “For the sake of Your servant David, do not reject Your anointed one.” It's a plain request, friends, and it's tied to David's name. Two short lines, and they carry a whole lot of asking.

The answer is one of his descendants. The LORD swore an oath to David, and the promise is, “One of your descendants I will place on your throne.” (Psalm 132:11). Notice it's called a promise He will not revoke, bakers. That's about as solid as a promise gets.

The answer is that their sons will sit on his throne forever. The LORD says, “If your sons keep My covenant and the testimony I will teach them, then their sons will also sit on your throne forever and ever.” The if is real, friends, and so is the promise that follows it. The reward goes past David's sons all the way to their sons.

The answer is His home. The song says, “For the LORD has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His home…” Chosen and desired, two warm words in one line, friends. A home is something you want, not just something you end up with.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have desired this home.” Forever and ever doesn't stop when David's life does, friends. The time limit in that statement just isn't in the verse.

The answer is poor. The LORD says, “I will satisfy her poor with bread.” Satisfy is a good word, friends, because it means more than just getting by. Bread is the one food in this line, so I'll leave it right there.

The answer is True. The song asked, “May Your priests be clothed with righteousness…” (Psalm 132:9), and the LORD says, “I will clothe her priests with salvation…” (Psalm 132:16). The first is a request for righteousness, and the LORD's own words speak of salvation, friends. Both times it's about the priests.
The answer is a lamp. The LORD says, “I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one.” Prepared is the word that caught my ear, friends. I know a little about getting something ready ahead of time.

The answer is shame for the first blank and gleam for the second. The LORD says, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but the crown upon him will gleam.” Notice the word clothe, bakers, so even the enemies get dressed in this song. Gleam is the word for the crown, and that's a nice way for a song to end.
